look_here_first: Both this species and Ludwigia repens have opposite leaves on creeping stems. Find an axillary flower: palustris has four green sepals and no yellow petals. Do not rely only on absent petals because repens may be apetalous or shed petals. Check the ovary/mature capsule: palustris typically has four longitudinal dark-green bands across its faces; repens does not.

key_traits.label: Habit
key_traits.text: Creeping/decumbent perennial of wet mud and shallow water; roots at nodes.

key_traits.label: Leaves
key_traits.text: Opposite, small elliptic to obovate, generally entire.

key_traits.label: Flower
key_traits.text: Minute axillary flowers with four usually green sepals; petals absent (not merely hidden). Usually four stamens.

key_traits.label: Fruit
key_traits.text: Short 2–5 mm 4-sided capsule with four green longitudinal bands, one across each face; compare with L. repens often longer 4–10 mm fruits that lack these characteristic bands. Fruit length overlaps and is supporting only.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: opposite leaves on creeping rooting stems shared with L. repens

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: petal-less tiny flower with four green sepals (repens sometimes loses/lacks petals too)

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: four dark-green longitudinal bands on ovary/capsule are the strongest confirmed separation from L. repens

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: short 2–5 mm capsule, though size overlaps repens

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: avoid guessing species from vegetative aquatic mats only
